h1: Collbran, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Collbran means evaluating more than a well permit. Local records show how deep wells are, what they have produced, how far water may be below ground, and what a new installation can cost. This page covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Collbran in Mesa County.

The records point to generally moderate well depths and useful reported yields, but the ground is not uniform. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, and nearby results can still vary. Check the specific parcel, neighboring wells, water rights, septic layout, and building plans before relying on a regional average.

sections.heading: Collbran well depths and the ground below
sections.html:
Collbran-area wells have a median reported depth of 98 feet. The middle half runs from 52 to 159 feet, so that range is a reasonable starting point when a driller prepares a bid, but it is not a guarantee for a particular lot. Half of the reported wells are under 100 feet, while 41% fall from 100 to 300 feet.

The deeper end matters for budgeting. The 90th-percentile depth is 280 feet, the deepest record reaches 1,000 feet, and 8% of wells are 300 to 600 feet. Another 1% are 600 feet or deeper. Ground here is described as mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, with 459 permits naming an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer and 15 naming alluvial water. Fractured rock can change quickly from one property to the next.

sections.heading: How much water Collbran wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 145 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 12.5 gallons per minute. The middle half is 7.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute, which is a useful range for comparing a driller’s estimate with nearby records. Reported production is not the same as a guaranteed long-term household supply, particularly where storage, pressure systems, or seasonal conditions affect use.

The yield mix is encouraging but uneven: 43% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 39% report more than 15. Another 16% fall between 1 and 5, while 1% are under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, and any history of low pressure or recovery problems. A permit’s allowed use also matters; most local permits are domestic or household wells, while stock and irrigation uses have different practical considerations.

sections.heading: Water levels and the Collbran trend
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth from the ground surface down to water when the well is not being pumped. The local median is 40 feet, with the middle half from 18 to 92 feet. That information helps a driller think about pump setting, trenching, and pressure-system design, but it does not tell you the water level in an untested parcel.

The decade figures deserve attention. The median measured water level was 36 feet below surface in the 2010s and 64 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper reported water level in the newer decade and may indicate changing conditions, although measurements can come from different wells, seasons, and pumping histories. Do not call it a confirmed area-wide decline without parcel-specific monitoring. For a purchase, obtain the well’s latest static level and ask how it behaves after sustained use.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Collbran, and when
sections.html:
The permit record shows long-term drilling activity around Collbran. Permits were issued in every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year being 2025. The busiest decades in the record were the 1990s with 88 permits and the 2000s with 89. There were 51 permits in the 2010s and 58 in the 2020s.

The most active names in these records are Rule, also listed as Rule, Leo A, with 48 wells; Wildcat Drilling & Pump, Inc., also listed as Kissner, Billy D., with 37; and Authorized, listed as Pe, Pg, with 30. These counts describe recorded work, not current availability or a quality ranking. Confirm a contractor’s current licensing, insurance, references, scope, and proposed testing before signing a drilling agreement.

sections.heading: What a new well costs around Collbran
sections.html:
For the local mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the 98-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $4,900 to $7,400. That figure is only the hole. Casing, grout, development, testing, and site access can change the final invoice.

A finished installation including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $10,900 to $19,400 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra trenching, or a different pump system can push the cost higher. Request a written bid that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, permits, testing, and any unsuccessful-hole terms. Compare bids using the same scope rather than the per-foot rate alone.

sections.heading: Collbran risks: water quality, low yield, and site layout
sections.html:
Low yield is a real but relatively uncommon result in the reported data: 1% of wells are under 1 gallon per minute, while 16% report 1 to 5. A dry hole is still possible because fractured-bedrock conditions can vary sharply over short distances. Neighboring wells are useful evidence, but they do not replace a site-specific investigation, pump test, and water-quality testing.

Environmental screening also deserves a close look. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 70 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. A map flag does not automatically mean a property’s water is unsafe, but it is a reason to test for the relevant contaminants and review agency records. Before building, confirm well-to-septic separation, reserve space for the septic system and replacement area, access for drilling equipment, and the electrical route.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Collbran lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact well permit, construction report, pump information, static water level, and water-quality results. Check how the neighboring wells on the same road perform, especially if the property lies in a fractured-bedrock setting. The regional median gives context, but the nearby records are more useful for estimating depth, yield, and water level on your lot.

Then confirm the legal water use before making an offer. Colorado permits control allowable use; an exempt household-use well generally has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and an over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan for certain uses. Have the driller, septic designer, electrician, and excavator review the site together. Build the budget around the finished system rather than drilling alone, and keep a contingency for deeper drilling, access work, testing, and site conditions.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Collbran, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Collbran is 98 feet. The middle half runs from 52 to 159 feet. Half are under 100 feet, but 41% are 100 to 300 feet, and the deepest record is 1,000 feet. Fractured-bedrock conditions mean a nearby well is useful evidence, not a promise for your parcel.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Collbran?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 98-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $4,900 to $7,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,900 to $19,400. Ask for a bid that clearly separates drilling from equipment and site work.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Collbran?
faq.a: Of the 145 local wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.5 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 7.0 to 15.0. However, 16% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 1% report under 1. Review the construction report and request a pump test before relying on a regional average.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Collbran?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 70 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the property’s water through an appropriate laboratory and review nearby environmental records before drinking it.

faq.q: Are Collbran well water levels dropping?
faq.a: Reported median static water level was 36 feet below surface in the 2010s and 64 feet in the 2020s. That deeper figure may suggest changing conditions, but the measurements can come from different wells, seasons, and pumping histories. Get the specific well’s current static level and ask for recovery information before buying.
